description: We are a group of students interested in technology, software development, data, and space science. This year, we are working on NASA’s “Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts” challenge. We welcome members interested in AI, data science, healthcare, space science, UI/UX, hardware, or software development who are eager to learn, contribute, and collaborate.
summary:
Astronomican is an astronaut health-monitoring prototype developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It brings astronaut health monitoring and mission-control oversight into one interface, featuring vital-sign displays, a visual body map, health-status indicators, rule-based alerts, response guidance, crew notifications, and an interactive mission timeline.

The project combines cited biomedical records from NASA's Apollo 15 mission with a separately labelled modern monitoring simulation to demonstrate how health concerns can be identified, communicated, and addressed during spaceflight. It distinguishes documented historical measurements from interpolated, estimated, and simulated values to maintain transparency and data integrity.

As human exploration moves toward longer missions and greater distances from Earth, astronauts will need better ways to monitor their health and coordinate responses with limited access to immediate medical support. Astronomican explores how accessible monitoring and decision-support software can contribute to safer, more informed space exploration.
details:
Overview

Astronomican is an astronaut health-monitoring and mission-control prototype developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It explores how astronaut health can be monitored, potential concerns identified, and responses coordinated during space missions.

How It Works

The application follows a five-step approach:

Monitor → Detect → Explain → Act → Record

It provides three main experiences:

1. Astronaut Dashboard

Displays individual crew health information, vital signs, a visual body map, health indicators, and daily check-ins.

2. Mission Control

Provides an overview of all three astronauts, including health readings, alerts, communication, and alert history.

3. Apollo 15 Simulation

Replays a 12-day historical mission using real biomedical records, 27 documented events, heart-rate visualizations, and an interactive mission timeline.

A rule-based alert system identifies unusual readings, presents response guidance, and allows crew members to notify and acknowledge one another. Mission Control can also communicate with astronauts through the prototype interface.

Creative Approach and Key Considerations

Our approach was to combine actual historical spaceflight biomedical records with the concept of a modern astronaut monitoring system. Instead of simply displaying numbers, Astronomican connects observations with their context, explains potential health concerns in accessible language, and demonstrates how astronauts and mission control could coordinate responses.

Data integrity was one of our primary considerations. Apollo 15's 1971 monitoring capabilities were considerably more limited than modern technology. We therefore distinguish between documented measurements, interpolated and estimated values, simulated modern parameters, and placeholder sensor readings. This ensures that demonstration data is never misrepresented as historical or actual sensor measurements.

We also considered mission context, such as physical exertion during EVAs, to avoid interpreting expected physiological changes as automatic health emergencies. The interface was designed to keep different types of information organized and accessible across desktop and mobile devices.

Technology and Development

The project was developed using:

  • HTML5, CSS3 and Vanilla JavaScript for the application structure, interface, monitoring logic, and interactions.
  • JSON and CSV for structured mission information, historical events, and telemetry.
  • SVG for custom charts, icons, and astronaut body-map visualizations.
  • GitHub for version control at Astronaut-Health-Monitor.
  • Vercel for deployment and web hosting at Project Astronomican.

The application runs directly in a web browser without additional installations or specialized hardware.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Astronauts operating far from Earth face limited access to immediate medical assistance. Transparent health monitoring, contextual alerts, and effective crew communication could help support better-informed decisions during these missions.

Astronomican demonstrates how historical biomedical data and modern monitoring concepts can be brought together in an accessible decision-support interface. Our goal is to explore how these ideas could contribute to astronaut wellbeing and safer space exploration, particularly during longer-duration missions.

Future development could include real wearable sensor integrations, clinically reviewed alert protocols, and more comprehensive monitoring of long-duration spaceflight health risks.

Disclaimer: Astronomican is an educational prototype, not a medical device or a substitute for professional medical guidance.
